answer:
Use \(1=\) open and \(0=\) closed, and write a state as \(ABCD\).

A shortest sequence is:

\[
A,\ B,\ A,\ C,\ A,\ B,\ A,\ D,\ A,\ B,\ A,\ C,\ A,\ B,\ A
\]

or, as one string,

\[
\boxed{ABACABADABACABA}
\]

The corresponding states are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{move} & ABCD\\\hline
0 & 0000\\
1 & 1000\quad(A)\\
2 & 1100\quad(B)\\
3 & 0100\quad(A)\\
4 & 0110\quad(C)\\
5 & 1110\quad(A)\\
6 & 1010\quad(B)\\
7 & 0010\quad(A)\\
8 & 0011\quad(D)\\
9 & 1011\quad(A)\\
10& 1111\quad(B)\\
11& 0111\quad(A)\\
12& 0101\quad(C)\\
13& 1101\quad(A)\\
14& 1001\quad(B)\\
15& 0001\quad(A)
\end{array}
\]

So the final state is \(0001\): only \(D\) is open.

To see that no shortcut exists, run breadth-first search from \(0000\). The first-discovery distances of the 16 states are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{distance} & \text{state}\\\hline
0&0000\\
1&1000\\
2&1100\\
3&0100\\
4&0110\\
5&1110\\
6&1010\\
7&0010\\
8&0011\\
9&1011\\
10&1111\\
11&0111\\
12&0101\\
13&1101\\
14&1001\\
15&0001
\end{array}
\]

Breadth-first search explores all states with fewer toggles before any state with more toggles. Since the target \(0001\) first appears at distance \(15\), no sequence of fewer than 15 legal toggles can reach it. Thus the sequence above is shortest.
